why.support: Every opinion comes from someone. Their job, values and life shape what they say. Some people gain if you agree. Ask: who's talking, and why?
why.core: Every opinion comes from somewhere. A person's job, values, background and experience shape what they say, and who they're saying it to. Some people gain if you agree with them. Working out who's talking, and why, helps you decide what to believe, at school, at work and when you vote.
why.extend: Opinions are shaped by the values, backgrounds and interests of the people who hold them. If you can spot perspective and bias, and name a text's purpose and audience, you can weigh claims fairly. You won't just accept or reject them on instinct.

articles.title: Every opinion comes from somewhere

body.support:
Ads, posts and speeches try to make you think something. Ask: *who's talking?*

**Values and life.** People's views come from their lives. A farmer, a nurse and a student might see the same thing in different ways. Their **values** (what matters most to them) shape what they say.

**Perspective and bias.** Everyone sees things from somewhere. That's their **perspective**. **Bias** is when someone only tells one side. They might skip facts that don't help them.

**Who gains?** Some people gain if you agree. They might get money or votes. That doesn't mean they're wrong. But check what they say.

**Purpose and audience.** Every text is made for a reason. That's its **purpose**. It's made for some people. That's its **audience**.

**Ask four questions**

1. **Who's talking?**
2. **What do they gain?**
3. **Who is it for?**
4. **What's missing?**

Sometimes a group's name hides who is behind it. Look for who paid for the ad.
body.core:
Ads, posts, speeches and letters to the editor all try to make you think something. Before you agree, ask: *who's talking?*

**Values and background.** People's opinions come from their lives. A farmer, a nurse, a business owner and a student might all see the same issue differently. Their **values** (what matters most to them) and their **background** (their job, culture, age and experience) shape what they notice and what they say.

**Perspective and bias.** Everyone has a **perspective**: the place they see an issue from. That's normal. **Bias** is when someone leans so far one way that they leave out the other side, or twist the facts. A biased text might:

- give only one side
- use facts that help them, and skip the rest
- describe the other side unfairly.

**Who gains?** Some people have a **vested interest**: they gain if you agree. That might be money, votes, power or a cause. It doesn't mean they're wrong. But it means you should check their claims.

**Purpose and audience.** Every text is made for a reason (**purpose**) and for certain people (**audience**). An ad aimed at parents will look and sound different from one aimed at teenagers.

**Four questions to ask**

1. **Who's talking?** What's their job, background and values?
2. **What do they gain** if you agree?
3. **Who's it for**, and what do they want you to think or do?
4. **What's missing?** Whose voice isn't there?

Sometimes the answer to *who's talking* isn't who it seems. A group's name can hide who's really behind it. So look for who paid for the ad, who runs the website, or who the speaker works for.
body.extend:
Persuasive and influential texts (advertisements, opinion columns, speeches, posts and letters) all aim to shape what an audience thinks or does. Evaluating them starts with the speaker.

**Values and background.** Opinions emerge from experience. A farmer, a nurse, a business owner and a student may interpret the same issue differently, because their **values** (what they consider most important) and **backgrounds** (occupation, culture, age, experience) shape what they notice and prioritise.

**Perspective and bias.** Every speaker has a **perspective**, a position from which they view an issue. **Bias** occurs when that position distorts the account: presenting one side only, selecting evidence that suits the argument, or misrepresenting opponents. Audiences bring their own biases too, which affect how they receive a message.

**Vested interests.** Speakers with a **vested interest** benefit if the audience agrees, whether financially, politically or ideologically. A vested interest doesn't make a claim false. It does mean the claim deserves closer scrutiny.

**Purpose and audience.** Every text has a **purpose** and an intended **audience**, and both shape its content, language and design.

**Four questions**

1. **Who's talking?** Background, role and values.
2. **What do they gain** from agreement?
3. **Who's the audience**, and what's the intended effect?
4. **What's missing?** Which perspectives are absent?

The apparent speaker isn't always the real one. **Front groups** present a cause under a neutral or grassroots name while concealing their funders. Check authorisation lines, ownership and funding.

caseStudies.title: The retailers who weren't just retailers

body.support:
In **2010**, the government said cigarettes would be sold in **plain packs**. No logos. No brand colours.

Then ads came out against the plan. They were from a group called the **Alliance of Australian Retailers**. It said it spoke for small shops.

But in **September 2010**, the ABC showed leaked papers. They showed the group was paid for by **big tobacco companies**.

The tobacco companies had a lot to lose. Their packs helped sell their brands.

The ads didn't work. Plain packs started in **December 2012**. Australia was the first country in the world to do it.

The lesson: a group's name doesn't always tell you who is talking. Ask who is paying.
body.core:
In **April 2010**, the federal government announced a world first. Cigarettes would be sold in **plain packs**, with no logos or brand colours.

Soon after, ads appeared in newspapers against the plan. They came from a group called the **Alliance of Australian Retailers**. It said it spoke for small shops, like corner stores, newsagents and service stations.

The ads looked like they came from local shopkeepers. But on **10 September 2010**, the ABC program **Lateline** revealed leaked documents. They showed the group had been set up with the help of tobacco company **Philip Morris** and a PR firm. And it was funded by three big tobacco companies: Philip Morris, British American Tobacco and Imperial Tobacco.

The tobacco companies had a lot to lose. Their packs were a key way to advertise their brands.

The campaign didn't stop the law. Tobacco companies challenged it in the **High Court**, and lost in 2012. Plain packaging started on **1 December 2012**. Australia was the first country in the world to do it.

The lesson: a group's name doesn't always tell you who's really talking. Ask who's paying.
body.extend:
In **April 2010**, the Rudd government announced a world first. Tobacco would be sold in **plain packaging**, with no logos, brand colours or images.

Within months, newspaper ads opposed the plan. They were authorised by the **Alliance of Australian Retailers**. The group said it spoke for small businesses: corner stores, newsagents and service stations worried about losing trade.

On **10 September 2010**, ABC TV's **Lateline** revealed leaked emails, contracts and documents. The alliance had been set up with **Philip Morris** and a PR firm. It was funded by Philip Morris, British American Tobacco and Imperial Tobacco. None of this was disclosed when the ads began.

The tobacco companies had a clear vested interest. Branded packs were one of the last ways they could still advertise in Australia.

The campaign failed. In **2012**, the **High Court** rejected a challenge by tobacco companies. Plain packaging began on **1 December 2012**.

The case shows how a front group can borrow a trusted voice, the local shopkeeper, to argue for someone else's interests.

model.text:
**The text:** A full-page newspaper ad that says “Keep our town moving. Say no to the bike lane.”

**Who is talking?** Small print at the bottom says “Authorised by the Main Street Traders Group”. They are shop owners.

**What do they want?** They want the council to keep the car parks out the front of their shops.

**Who are they talking to?** Local drivers and voters. The ad says “our town” and “your car park”.

**What might they leave out?** How many people ride. Whether bike lanes are safer. What people who do not drive think.

teacher.overview: The first course in Issues & Voices. Students learn how the values, backgrounds and interests of authors and speakers shape their opinions; the difference between perspective and bias; and how to identify the purpose and audience of persuasive texts. They annotate a made-up letter to the editor, sort claims, map stakeholder perspectives, and investigate a real opinion text. The case study is the Alliance of Australian Retailers, a 2010 campaign against plain packaging that presented itself as small shopkeepers but was revealed by ABC Lateline to be funded by tobacco companies.
prep: Gather a few current opinion texts on issues students care about (letters to the editor, opinion columns, ads, posts).
Optional: find an image of an Australian plain cigarette pack to show.
Show students where to find authorisation lines on ads and “About us” pages on websites.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** values and background shape what people notice, care about and say. Everyone has a perspective; bias leaves out or twists other sides. Who's talking? What do they gain? Who's it for? What's missing?

**Letter:** 1 the opinion (close at 6pm); 2 who's talking (café owner next door); 3 values (family, quiet, safety); 4 vested interest (noise affects his business); 5 bias (sweeping claim, no evidence, skaters' voices missing); 6 purpose and audience (wants councillors to vote yes).

**Sort:** phone ad — bias; BoM — fair; car park owner — bias; split news report — fair; gambling app — bias; student group — bias.

**Case study:** the ads seemed to come from small shopkeepers; leaked documents showed tobacco companies created and funded the group. A shopkeeper is more sympathetic than a tobacco company. Knowing the funder reveals a vested interest, so the claims need checking.

realityCheck: **Students may decide everyone is biased, so nothing can be trusted.** Push back: perspective is normal; the goal is to weigh claims, not dismiss them.
**Keep it non-partisan.** Use the four questions on texts from different sides of an issue.
**Finding funders is hard.** Model checking authorisation lines and “About us” pages.
**The case is old for students.** Link it to now: who pays for the ads and influencers they see?
**Works in a real class:** yes. The four questions transfer to every other course in this zone.
